name: Placebo Effect
description: Expectations and treatment context can change what people actually feel or report, even when the intervention itself is inert. But the broad popular idea of a placebo 'working' across all outcomes is stronger than the best evidence supports.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to onboarding promises, wellness and health products, premium framing, device rituals, support experiences, and any interaction that sets expectations before the core experience unfolds.
myth_risk_note: The popular framing of the placebo effect as a broadly powerful, near-universal healing mechanism overstates the evidence -- Kienle & Kiene's reanalysis of the foundational Beecher claim found much of the apparent effect is attributable to natural history and regression to the mean rather than a true psychobiological effect, and Hrobjartsson & Gotzsche's meta-analysis (already in the corpus) similarly found no significant effect on objective outcomes in most trials. Real neurobiological and subjective-symptom effects remain well-documented (Price et al. 2007; neuroimaging studies), just narrower in scope than the popular framing implies.
prevalence_note: A very widely recognized term in health, wellness, service, and marketing conversations, and familiar enough in product work to shape expectation-design decisions even when it is not named as a formal UX heuristic.

findings.description: Across clinical trials comparing placebo with no treatment, placebo interventions did not show strong clinically important effects across most objective or binary outcomes, though some patient-reported continuous outcomes — especially pain-related ones — could still move. The broad popular idea of a universal placebo effect is therefore overstated relative to the highest-rigor review evidence.
findings.source_title: Placebo interventions for all clinical conditions

findings.description: Placebo and placebo-related effects are real biopsychosocial phenomena: treatment context and expectation can trigger specific biochemical and cellular changes that alter symptoms and therapy response. But the mechanisms vary by domain, so this is not evidence for a single simple placebo law that applies equally everywhere.
findings.source_title: Mechanisms of Placebo and Placebo-Related Effects Across Diseases and Treatments
findings.source_venue: Annual Review of Pharmacology and Toxicology

applications.title: A disputed meta-analysis claiming placebo explains 69% of clinical-trial treatment effects, under journal investigation
applications.description: A paper by Harald Walach and coauthors, published December 2025 in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, analyzed 30 clinical trials each across five conditions (osteoarthritis, depression, migraines, sleep disorders, irritable bowel syndrome) and concluded the placebo effect 'alone explains 69% of the variance' in treatment effects. Named critics (Stephen Rhodes, in a published letter to the editor; Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz, interviewed by Retraction Watch) identified a fundamental misunderstanding of what a placebo-controlled 'treatment effect' measures, an inability to replicate the stated methodology, the inclusion of a trial retracted in 2018 for a randomization fraud, and an undisclosed conflict of interest (Walach runs an institute promoting homeopathy). The journal is actively investigating the paper following Retraction Watch's inquiry.
applications.ethical_note: This is a research-integrity case about a disputed scientific claim regarding the placebo effect itself, not a product or interface applying the placebo effect to influence users -- there is no persuasion or UX design dimension here. Included because it strengthens this corpus's thinnest cluster (Evidentiary Rigor & Meta-Science) with a genuine, well-documented, still-unfolding case directly relevant to the placebo-effect topic, following the same discipline already used for the Ariely/Wertenbroch retraction.

applications.title: Placebos can work even when patients know they're placebos -- but not for people with frontal-lobe damage
applications.description: Contrary to the assumption that deception is essential to the placebo effect, research shows patients can experience genuine symptom relief from a placebo even when explicitly told it is one, if the interaction with their health provider primes them appropriately. The effect is not universal, however: placebo pain relief is significantly reduced in people with frontal-lobe damage, including stroke survivors, brain-injury patients, and people with dementia.
applications.ethical_note: Directly undercuts the popular myth that the placebo effect 'only works on the gullible' or requires deception -- relevant to this graph's own myth-risk-flagging mission, since design or wellness content citing the placebo effect as evidence that expectation/belief alone drives outcomes should account for the real, disclosed boundary conditions (frontal-lobe function) this source describes rather than treating it as a universal, purely psychological phenomenon.
